title: Distinctions of necessity: absolute and hypothetical; of coaction and of infallibility
source_text: XXXI. Ut vero necessitatem illam, quam Dei decretum quibuslibet eventibus imponit, cum eorum contingentia & libertate concilient, distinguunt primo inter necessitatem absolutam & necessitatem quae est ex hypothesi. Necessitas absoluta est qua simpliciter aliquid aliter esse non potest. Necessitas autem ex hypothesi est, qua quod in se & simpliciter potest non esse, vel aliter esse, posita tamen certa conditione, aliter se habere non potest. Deinde necessitas ab ipsis distinguitur in eam quae est coactionis, & eam quae est tantum infallibilitatis. Necessitas coactionis est, quae per causam extra agentem vim rebus infert, & coacte impellit ut hoc vel illud faciant. Necessitas vero infallibilitatis est, qua res quoad eventum certo & immutabiliter futura est: ita tamen ut si causam rei per se spectemus, possit vel non evenire, vel aliter evenire. Qua de necessitate intelligendum est illud axioma, Omne quod est, dum est, necessario est.
pass_a_gloss: XXXI. But that they may reconcile that necessity, which the decree of God imposes on any events whatever, with their contingency and freedom, they distinguish first between absolute necessity and the necessity which is from hypothesis. Absolute necessity is that by which something simply cannot be otherwise. But necessity from hypothesis is that by which what in itself and simply can not be, or be otherwise, yet a certain condition being posited, cannot be otherwise. Then necessity is distinguished by them into that which is of coaction, and that which is only of infallibility. Necessity of coaction is that which through a cause acting from outside brings force on things, and impels them by compulsion to do this or that. But necessity of infallibility is that by which a thing as to its event is certainly and immutably future: yet so that if we regard the cause of the thing in itself, it can either not come about, or come about otherwise. Of which necessity that axiom is to be understood, Everything that is, while it is, necessarily is.
pass_b_english: To reconcile the necessity that God's decree places on every event with the contingency and freedom of those events, they first distinguish absolute necessity from necessity on a hypothesis. Absolute necessity is that by which something simply cannot be otherwise. Necessity on a hypothesis is that by which something that in itself and simply can fail to be, or be otherwise, cannot be otherwise once a certain condition is given.

Next they divide necessity into the necessity of coercion and the necessity of mere infallibility. The necessity of coercion is that by which a cause acting from outside applies force to things and drives them by compulsion to do this or that.

The necessity of infallibility is that by which a thing is certainly and unchangeably going to happen, yet such that, if we look at the thing's cause in itself, it could fail to happen or happen otherwise. This is the necessity meant in the axiom, 'Everything that is, while it is, is necessarily.'
